```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(readxl)
library(urca)
library(vars)
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "C"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")

raw <- read_excel("tether_market_dominance.xlsx")
raw$date <- as.Date(raw$timeClose)
sample <- subset(raw, date >= as.Date("2020-01-01") & date < as.Date("2024-01-01"))
sample <- sample[order(sample$date), ]
stopifnot(nrow(sample) > 20, all(diff(as.integer(sample$date)) == 7),
          all(is.finite(sample$crypto_volatility_index)), all(sample$crypto_volatility_index > 0),
          all(is.finite(sample$global_market_dominance)), all(sample$global_market_dominance > 0))

# The workbook stores market share as a fraction. A value of 0.03 means three percent.
sample$share_pct <- 100 * sample$global_market_dominance
vol <- ts(log(sample$crypto_volatility_index))
share <- ts(log(sample$share_pct))
d_vol <- diff(vol)
d_share <- diff(share)
d2_share <- diff(share, differences = 2)
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

## Two views of the same market

USDT dominance is the market capitalisation of Tether divided by the total crypto market capitalisation. A change in that ratio can come from either side. I wanted to know whether the recent path of crypto volatility contains information about subsequent changes in dominance, and whether the reverse relationship also appears in the data.

I matched Tether market share to the Crypto Volatility Index. The original study set its cutoff at the end of 2023. The workbook supplies **`r nrow(sample)` consecutive weekly observations** from **`r format(min(sample$date), "%d %B %Y")`** to **`r format(max(sample$date), "%d %B %Y")`** within that window.

```{r levels, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4.2, 1.4, 1), las = 1, mgp = c(2.6, 0.6, 0))
plot(sample$date, sample$crypto_volatility_index, type = "l", lwd = 1.7,
     col = "#235E73", xlab = "", ylab = "Index level", main = "Crypto Volatility Index")
plot(sample$date, sample$share_pct, type = "l", lwd = 1.7, col = "#9A5938",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Market share (%)", main = "Tether dominance")
```

The original workbook combines the [Crypto Volatility Index](https://www.investing.com/indices/crypto-volatility-index-historical-data), [Tether market capitalisation](https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/tether/historical-data/) and [total crypto market capitalisation](https://www.coingecko.com/en/global-charts).

\newpage

## Choosing the series to model

The coursework used a first difference of log volatility and a second difference of log dominance. I retained these transformations so the main result can be reproduced. A second difference describes the change in the weekly growth rate of market share.

```{r stationarity}
diagnostics <- function(x) {
  adf <- ur.df(x, type = "drift", lags = 1)
  kpss <- ur.kpss(x, type = "mu", lags = "short")
  # The packages store several cutoffs. Read the five percent column by name.
  c(ADF = adf@teststat[1, "tau2"], "ADF cutoff" = adf@cval["tau2", "5pct"],
    KPSS = as.numeric(kpss@teststat), "KPSS cutoff" = kpss@cval[1, "5pct"])
}
series <- list("Log volatility" = vol, "Change in log volatility" = d_vol,
               "Log dominance" = share, "Change in log dominance" = d_share,
               "Second change in log dominance" = d2_share)
stationarity <- t(vapply(series, diagnostics, numeric(4)))
knitr::kable(stationarity, digits = 3)
```

The ADF test rejects a unit root below its cutoff. The KPSS test rejects level stationarity above its cutoff. The tests ask different questions, and differencing is a modelling choice in this short sample.

## A short forecast

```{r forecast}
ma1 <- forecast::Arima(d2_share, order = c(0, 0, 1), method = "CSS-ML")
# One MA coefficient was fitted, so we subtract one degree of freedom in this test.
ljung <- Box.test(residuals(ma1), lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 1)
prediction <- forecast::forecast(ma1, h = 3, level = 95)
forecast_table <- data.frame(
  Week = as.character(max(sample$date) + 7 * seq_len(3)),
  Forecast = as.numeric(prediction$mean),
  Lower = as.numeric(prediction$lower), Upper = as.numeric(prediction$upper)
)
knitr::kable(forecast_table, digits = 4)
```

The MA(1) forecast is expressed in second differences of log dominance. The bands are 95 percent prediction intervals in the same units. The Ljung-Box test on the residuals at 20 lags gives p = `r fmt(ljung$p.value)`.

\newpage

## Which series moves first?

```{r var}
# A second difference needs an extra week. Line up both series before fitting the VAR.
pair <- ts.intersect(vol_change = d_vol, share_acceleration = d2_share)
lag_choice <- VARselect(pair, lag.max = 15, type = "const")$selection
model <- VAR(pair, p = 3, type = "const")
vol_leads <- causality(model, cause = "vol_change")$Granger
share_leads <- causality(model, cause = "share_acceleration")$Granger
tests <- data.frame(
  "Predictor" = c("Changes in log volatility", "Changes in log dominance growth"),
  "Target" = c("Changes in log dominance growth", "Changes in log volatility"),
  "p-value" = c(vol_leads$p.value, share_leads$p.value), check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tests, digits = 4)
```

AIC selects `r unname(lag_choice["AIC(n)"])` lags and Schwarz selects `r unname(lag_choice["SC(n)"])`. I used the three-lag specification with an intercept from the coursework. Past changes in volatility helped predict changes in Tether's market share growth at the five percent level. The reverse test gives p = `r fmt(share_leads$p.value)`. The tests describe predictive timing in this sample. They cannot identify why someone bought or sold USDT.

```{r response, fig.width=6.8, fig.height=2.65}
# Put volatility first, as in the coursework. This ordering matters for a same-week shock.
response <- irf(model, impulse = "vol_change", response = "share_acceleration",
                n.ahead = 12, ortho = TRUE, ci = 0.95, runs = 499, seed = 2024)
horizon <- 0:12
centre <- drop(response$irf$vol_change)
lower <- drop(response$Lower$vol_change)
upper <- drop(response$Upper$vol_change)
par(mar = c(3.6, 4.6, 1.2, 0.7), mgp = c(2.8, 0.6, 0), las = 1)
plot(horizon, centre, type = "n", ylim = range(lower, upper, 0),
     xlab = "Weeks after the volatility shock", ylab = "Log-share response")
polygon(c(horizon, rev(horizon)), c(lower, rev(upper)), border = NA, col = "#DEEAED")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey55", lty = 2)
lines(horizon, centre, lwd = 2, col = "#235E73")
```

The shaded area shows the 95 percent bootstrap interval for a one-standard-deviation volatility shock. Under this ordering, the response changes sign after the first week and then moves back towards zero. The band reflects estimation uncertainty in this sample.
